theme: I do not rebuke you for sacrifices, what God truly desires
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 50. After weeks of reading about sacrifices, this psalm puts a question to them. Read it as God’s own voice, speaking in court, about what he truly wants from his people.
settingTheScene: Psalm 50 is a psalm of Asaph, one of the leaders of music in David’s time. It is set in a courtroom. God summons the earth as a witness and speaks against his people. But the psalm does not say that the sacrifices were wrong. It says that Israel had begun to treat them as a way of handling God, as if he needed them. In the setting of the book of Leviticus, the psalm is a needed correction. It asks what the sacrifices were meant to do.
observation: “The Mighty One, God the LORD, speaks and summons the earth from the rising of the sun to its setting” (v. 1).
“Out of Zion, the perfection of beauty, God shines forth” (v. 2).
God says he will speak to his people: “Gather to me my faithful ones, who made a covenant with me by sacrifice!” (v. 5).
“I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices; your burnt offerings are continually before me” (v. 8).
“If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine” (v. 12).
“Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and perform your vows to the Most High” (v. 14).
“Call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (v. 15).

To the wicked God says, “What right have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips?” (vv. 16-21). The psalm ends: “The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me” (v. 23).
interpretation:
The psalm does not criticize the sacrifices themselves. God says, “I do not rebuke you for your sacrifices.” What he corrects is a wrong idea about them. Some in Israel had come to think that the sacrifices fed God, or that they put him in their debt. God answers with a bit of humor: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you.” The cattle on a thousand hills are his. He does not need anything from us.

This is a necessary lesson for any religion. It is easy to think that our worship is a favor to God. The truth is the opposite. We need him, and he does not need us. Sacrifice does not make God our debtor. It is a way for us to receive from him.

What God wants, in place of a misunderstanding of sacrifice, is thanksgiving. “Offer to God a sacrifice of thanksgiving.” The word is todah, and it also names a kind of peace offering, the thanksgiving offering of Leviticus 7:12. God wants his people to come with gratitude, to keep their vows, and to call on him in trouble. The relationship is one of dependence and thanks.

The second half of the psalm turns to people who go through the motions but live wickedly. They recite God’s laws, but they steal, commit adultery, and slander. God’s response is sharp. He has been silent, and they have assumed that he was like them, but now he will confront them. The warning is that formal religion without a changed life is dangerous.

The last verse puts the two halves together: “The one who offers thanksgiving as his sacrifice glorifies me; to one who orders his way rightly I will show the salvation of God.” Thanksgiving and a right way of life belong together. This is the heart behind the sacrifice.
connection: Paul told the Athenians that God is not “served by human hands, as though he needed anything” (Acts 17:25). Hebrews 13:15 says, “Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name.” Jesus said that the people honored him with their lips but their hearts were far away (Mark 7:6). Paul says that we are to “give thanks in all circumstances” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).
application:
Thank God today for five specific things, aloud. Treat it as an offering.

Ask whether your religion has become a way of handling God, rather than receiving from him.

Consider whether your life matches the words you say in worship.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he needs nothing from you yet receives your thanks.
Ask him to keep you from empty religion.
Ask him to let your life match your words.
